finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header without any verification, so any client that can reach the app directly can impersonate any user holding grants and delete or rename their files.
finding.sink: views.py:17-18 ensure_allowed + del STORE[fid]; views.py:25-27 is_allowed + mutation of f["name"]

trace.note: header read into g.user with no signature/gateway check
is_allowed looks up resource['grants'][user]; trusts whatever identity was supplied
rename_file uses the same unverified identity for the write check

finding.guards_checked: acl.py:5 denies when header is absent (get(None, []) -> []), so missing header is not a bypass; per-file grant checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 are enforced but only against the claimed identity; no code in these files verifies or strips the header. Whether exploitable depends on ingress behavior not visible here.

verdict.guard_found: views.py:17 ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 on failure and its result is not discarded; views.py:25 is_allowed result is tested at views.py:25-26; acl.py:5 returns False when the header is absent. Neither guard verifies the identity itself, so they only enforce grants against whatever value the header supplies.
verdict.reason: All trace lines match (views.py:11, 17-18, 25; acl.py:5), and nothing in views.py or acl.py verifies or strips X-Session-User-Verified, but the directory contains no ingress, proxy, or deployment config (only views.py and acl.py exist), so whether a client can reach the app with that header set directly is undetermined.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs raise KeyError (HTTP 500) before any authorization check, while existing-but-unauthorized IDs return 403, letting any client enumerate which file IDs exist.
finding.source: views.py:15 and views.py:23 path parameter fid, reachable by any actor including unauthenticated (g.user None)
finding.sink: views.py:16 and views.py:24 STORE[fid] evaluated before authz

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown fid -> 500
abort(403) for existing but unauthorized fid

finding.guards_checked: fid is only a dict key, so no traversal or injection; authz is enforced for existing IDs; no existence-independent response exists, so the 500 vs 403 difference is an oracle.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the lookup. load_user (views.py:9-11) only sets g.user from a header and does not reject anonymous requests. STORE[fid] at views.py:16 and views.py:24 runs before any authz call. The only authz controls are ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, which calls abort(403) on failure) at views.py:17 and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, checked at views.py:25) for rename. Both run only after the lookup, so they cannot stop the unknown-ID KeyError. Existing-but-unauthorized IDs get 403 at acl.py:10 and views.py:26, so the 500 vs 403 difference is observable.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: views.py:16 and views.py:24 index STORE before authz, so an unknown fid raises KeyError (HTTP 500 under Flask) while an existing fid reaches ensure_allowed at views.py:17 and aborts with 403 at acl.py:10, and the same split appears on rename at views.py:24-26. Anonymous requests reach this because load_user at views.py:9-11 does not reject a missing header, so the ID-existence oracle is reachable without any role. The impact is low (it reveals only which random IDs exist, not contents), so severity should stay low.
